newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians brace for tough 1997 budget medicine.
newsitem.headline: Italians brace for tough 1997 budget medicine.

text.p: Italy was set to approve a tough budget on Friday to halve its deficit and speed the country to join a single European currency, but economists fear the measures could land the economy in full-blown recession.

A government source said the 1997 budget package would aim to slice a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's public sector deficit, making it one of the most ambitious in recent years.
The main portion of the budget would comprise 25 trillion lire in spending cuts and 12.5 trillion lire in fresh revenues.

A further 12.5 trillion lire would be raised from a once-off "Euro-tax" and another 12.5 trillion from unspecified "treasury operations". Full details were expected to be disclosed after a cabinet meeting being chaired by Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
Economists said a hefty dose of new taxes could deal a body-blow to an economy that is already struggling in the face of flat consumer demand and flagging exports.
The government says it is counting on the central bank to deliver a string of interest rate cuts that will reduce the cost of borrowing money in time to make up for the fiscal tightening.

"On the growth side, a package of this size will have dire consequences," said Sally Wilkinson, a London-based economist at Swiss bank UBS. "To impose a severe fiscal package at a time of slow growth and an appreciating currency would be suicide."

"It's clear the Euro tax would lower consumption and with the economy already practically in recession the situation could become dangerous," said another economist at an international investment bank in London who asked not to be named.

Italian bond markets and the lira have soared in recent days on a tidal wave of optimism over Italy's chances of meeting strict qualifying criteria for membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 1999.

Diego Masi, the parliamentary leader of Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini's centrist Italian Renewal party, resigned in protest on Friday saying the government had caved in to pressure from hard-left leader Fausto Bertinotti.

Prodi has quietly shelved plans to tax pensions and raise charges for hospital treatment after Bertinotti threatened to scupper the budget in parliament. The centre-left government relies on support from Bertinotti's Marxist-inspired Communist Refoundation in the lower house.

The planned budget is far in excess of the 32.4 trillion lire the government originally intended to shave from the public sector deficit and aims to cut Italy's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio to three percent by the end of next year.
Achievement of the three percent deficit target would put Italy on course to join an advance party of countries establishing a single European currency in 1999.
If the budget were to accelerate the economic slowdown, Italy would face falling tax revenues making it even harder to close a deficit which is heading for six percent at the end of this year.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in a front-page article in Friday's Corriere della Sera daily that Italy had to deliver a credible budget if it wanted to secure a lasting fall in interest rates.
"We have a duty to generate credibility. It is the path to reduce interest rates and therefore the deficit," Ciampi said.
A Reuter survey of 12 economists showed on Friday that the Bank of Italy is expected to cut the official discount rate by the end of October from its current level of 8.25 percent.
